[1366](https://docs.rs#1366)    /// Removes and returns the key and value corresponding to the most recently
[1367](https://docs.rs#1367)    /// used item or `None` if the cache is empty.
[1368](https://docs.rs#1368)    ///
[1369](https://docs.rs#1369)    /// # Example
[1370](https://docs.rs#1370)    ///
[1371](https://docs.rs#1371)    /// ```
[1372](https://docs.rs#1372)    /// use lru::LruCache;
[1373](https://docs.rs#1373)    /// use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
[1374](https://docs.rs#1374)    /// let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
[1375](https://docs.rs#1375)    ///
[1376](https://docs.rs#1376)    /// cache.put(2, "a");
[1377](https://docs.rs#1377)    /// cache.put(3, "b");
[1378](https://docs.rs#1378)    /// cache.put(4, "c");
[1379](https://docs.rs#1379)    /// cache.get(&3);
[1380](https://docs.rs#1380)    ///
[1381](https://docs.rs#1381)    /// assert_eq!(cache.pop_mru(), Some((3, "b")));
[1382](https://docs.rs#1382)    /// assert_eq!(cache.pop_mru(), Some((4, "c")));
[1383](https://docs.rs#1383)    /// assert_eq!(cache.pop_mru(), None);
[1384](https://docs.rs#1384)    /// assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
[1385](https://docs.rs#1385)    /// ```
[1386](https://docs.rs#1386)    pub fn pop_mru(&mut self) -> Option<(K, V)> {
[1387](https://docs.rs#1387)        let node = self.remove_first()?;
[1388](https://docs.rs#1388)        // N.B.: Can't destructure directly because of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/28536
[1389](https://docs.rs#1389)        let node = *node;
[1390](https://docs.rs#1390)        let LruEntry { key, val, .. } = node;
[1391](https://docs.rs#1391)        unsafe { Some((key.assume_init(), val.assume_init())) }
[1392](https://docs.rs#1392)    }
[1393](https://docs.rs#1393)
[1394](https://docs.rs#1394)    /// Marks the key as the most recently used one. Returns true if the key
[1395](https://docs.rs#1395)    /// was promoted because it exists in the cache, false otherwise.
[1396](https://docs.rs#1396)    ///
[1397](https://docs.rs#1397)    /// # Example
[1398](https://docs.rs#1398)    ///
[1399](https://docs.rs#1399)    /// ```
[1400](https://docs.rs#1400)    /// use lru::LruCache;
[1401](https://docs.rs#1401)    /// use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
[1402](https://docs.rs#1402)    /// let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
[1403](https://docs.rs#1403)    ///
[1404](https://docs.rs#1404)    /// cache.put(1, "a");
[1405](https://docs.rs#1405)    /// cache.put(2, "b");
[1406](https://docs.rs#1406)    /// cache.put(3, "c");
[1407](https://docs.rs#1407)    /// cache.get(&1);
[1408](https://docs.rs#1408)    /// cache.get(&2);
[1409](https://docs.rs#1409)    ///
[1410](https://docs.rs#1410)    /// // If we do `pop_lru` now, we would pop 3.
[1411](https://docs.rs#1411)    /// // assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((3, "c")));
[1412](https://docs.rs#1412)    ///
[1413](https://docs.rs#1413)    /// // By promoting 3, we make sure it isn't popped.
[1414](https://docs.rs#1414)    /// assert!(cache.promote(&3));
[1415](https://docs.rs#1415)    /// assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((1, "a")));
[1416](https://docs.rs#1416)    ///
[1417](https://docs.rs#1417)    /// // Promoting an entry that doesn't exist doesn't do anything.
[1418](https://docs.rs#1418)    /// assert!(!cache.promote(&4));
[1419](https://docs.rs#1419)    /// ```
[1420](https://docs.rs#1420)    pub fn promote<Q>(&mut self, k: &Q) -> bool
[1421](https://docs.rs#1421)    where
[1422](https://docs.rs#1422)        K: Borrow<Q>,
[1423](https://docs.rs#1423)        Q: Hash + Eq + ?Sized,
[1424](https://docs.rs#1424)    {
[1425](https://docs.rs#1425)        if let Some(node) = self.map.get_mut(KeyWrapper::from_ref(k)) {
[1426](https://docs.rs#1426)            let node_ptr: *mut LruEntry<K, V> = node.as_ptr();
[1427](https://docs.rs#1427)            self.detach(node_ptr);
[1428](https://docs.rs#1428)            self.attach(node_ptr);
[1429](https://docs.rs#1429)            true
[1430](https://docs.rs#1430)        } else {
[1431](https://docs.rs#1431)            false
[1432](https://docs.rs#1432)        }
[1433](https://docs.rs#1433)    }
[1434](https://docs.rs#1434)
[1435](https://docs.rs#1435)    /// Marks the key as the least recently used one. Returns true if the key was demoted
[1436](https://docs.rs#1436)    /// because it exists in the cache, false otherwise.
[1437](https://docs.rs#1437)    ///
[1438](https://docs.rs#1438)    /// # Example
[1439](https://docs.rs#1439)    ///
[1440](https://docs.rs#1440)    /// ```
[1441](https://docs.rs#1441)    /// use lru::LruCache;
[1442](https://docs.rs#1442)    /// use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
[1443](https://docs.rs#1443)    /// let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
[1444](https://docs.rs#1444)    ///
[1445](https://docs.rs#1445)    /// cache.put(1, "a");
[1446](https://docs.rs#1446)    /// cache.put(2, "b");
[1447](https://docs.rs#1447)    /// cache.put(3, "c");
[1448](https://docs.rs#1448)    /// cache.get(&1);
[1449](https://docs.rs#1449)    /// cache.get(&2);
[1450](https://docs.rs#1450)    ///
[1451](https://docs.rs#1451)    /// // If we do `pop_lru` now, we would pop 3.
[1452](https://docs.rs#1452)    /// // assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((3, "c")));
[1453](https://docs.rs#1453)    ///
[1454](https://docs.rs#1454)    /// // By demoting 1 and 2, we make sure those are popped first.
[1455](https://docs.rs#1455)    /// assert!(cache.demote(&2));
[1456](https://docs.rs#1456)    /// assert!(cache.demote(&1));
[1457](https://docs.rs#1457)    /// assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((1, "a")));
[1458](https://docs.rs#1458)    /// assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((2, "b")));
[1459](https://docs.rs#1459)    ///
[1460](https://docs.rs#1460)    /// // Demoting a key that doesn't exist does nothing.
[1461](https://docs.rs#1461)    /// assert!(!cache.demote(&4));
[1462](https://docs.rs#1462)    /// ```
[1463](https://docs.rs#1463)    pub fn demote<Q>(&mut self, k: &Q) -> bool
[1464](https://docs.rs#1464)    where
[1465](https://docs.rs#1465)        K: Borrow<Q>,
[1466](https://docs.rs#1466)        Q: Hash + Eq + ?Sized,
[1467](https://docs.rs#1467)    {
[1468](https://docs.rs#1468)        if let Some(node) = self.map.get_mut(KeyWrapper::from_ref(k)) {
[1469](https://docs.rs#1469)            let node_ptr: *mut LruEntry<K, V> = node.as_ptr();
[1470](https://docs.rs#1470)            self.detach(node_ptr);
[1471](https://docs.rs#1471)            self.attach_last(node_ptr);
[1472](https://docs.rs#1472)            true
[1473](https://docs.rs#1473)        } else {
[1474](https://docs.rs#1474)            false
[1475](https://docs.rs#1475)        }
[1476](https://docs.rs#1476)    }

[1532](https://docs.rs#1532)    /// Resizes the cache. If the new capacity is smaller than the size of the current
[1533](https://docs.rs#1533)    /// cache any entries past the new capacity are discarded.
[1534](https://docs.rs#1534)    ///
[1535](https://docs.rs#1535)    /// # Example
[1536](https://docs.rs#1536)    ///
[1537](https://docs.rs#1537)    /// ```
[1538](https://docs.rs#1538)    /// use lru::LruCache;
[1539](https://docs.rs#1539)    /// use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
[1540](https://docs.rs#1540)    /// let mut cache: LruCache<isize, &str> = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
[1541](https://docs.rs#1541)    ///
[1542](https://docs.rs#1542)    /// cache.put(1, "a");
[1543](https://docs.rs#1543)    /// cache.put(2, "b");
[1544](https://docs.rs#1544)    /// cache.resize(NonZeroUsize::new(4).unwrap());
[1545](https://docs.rs#1545)    /// cache.put(3, "c");
[1546](https://docs.rs#1546)    /// cache.put(4, "d");
[1547](https://docs.rs#1547)    ///
[1548](https://docs.rs#1548)    /// assert_eq!(cache.len(), 4);
[1549](https://docs.rs#1549)    /// assert_eq!(cache.get(&1), Some(&"a"));
[1550](https://docs.rs#1550)    /// assert_eq!(cache.get(&2), Some(&"b"));
[1551](https://docs.rs#1551)    /// assert_eq!(cache.get(&3), Some(&"c"));
[1552](https://docs.rs#1552)    /// assert_eq!(cache.get(&4), Some(&"d"));
[1553](https://docs.rs#1553)    /// ```
[1554](https://docs.rs#1554)    pub fn resize(&mut self, cap: NonZeroUsize) {
[1555](https://docs.rs#1555)        // return early if capacity doesn't change
[1556](https://docs.rs#1556)        if cap == self.cap {
[1557](https://docs.rs#1557)            return;
[1558](https://docs.rs#1558)        }
[1559](https://docs.rs#1559)
[1560](https://docs.rs#1560)        while self.map.len() > cap.get() {
[1561](https://docs.rs#1561)            self.pop_lru();
[1562](https://docs.rs#1562)        }
[1563](https://docs.rs#1563)        self.map.shrink_to_fit();
[1564](https://docs.rs#1564)
[1565](https://docs.rs#1565)        self.cap = cap;
[1566](https://docs.rs#1566)    }
[1567](https://docs.rs#1567)

[1576](https://docs.rs#1576)    /// assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
[1577](https://docs.rs#1577)    ///

[1579](https://docs.rs#1579)    /// assert_eq!(cache.len(), 1);

[1587](https://docs.rs#1587)    pub fn clear(&mut self) {
[1588](https://docs.rs#1588)        while self.pop_lru().is_some() {}
[1589](https://docs.rs#1589)    }

[1591](https://docs.rs#1591)    /// An iterator visiting all entries in most-recently used order. The iterator element type is

[1597](https://docs.rs#1597)    /// use lru::LruCache;

[1599](https://docs.rs#1599)    ///
[1600](https://docs.rs#1600)    /// let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());

[1602](https://docs.rs#1602)    /// cache.put("b", 2);

[1605](https://docs.rs#1605)    /// for (key, val) in cache.iter() {
[1606](https://docs.rs#1606)    ///     println!("key: {} val: {}", key, val);
[1607](https://docs.rs#1607)    /// }
[1608](https://docs.rs#1608)    /// ```
[1609](https://docs.rs#1609)    pub fn iter(&self) -> Iter<'_, K, V> {
[1610](https://docs.rs#1610)        Iter {
[1611](https://docs.rs#1611)            len: self.len(),
[1612](https://docs.rs#1612)            ptr: unsafe { (*self.head).next },
[1613](https://docs.rs#1613)            end: unsafe { (*self.tail).prev },
[1614](https://docs.rs#1614)            phantom: PhantomData,
[1615](https://docs.rs#1615)        }
[1616](https://docs.rs#1616)    }

[1618](https://docs.rs#1618)    /// An iterator visiting all entries in most-recently-used order, giving a mutable reference on
[1619](https://docs.rs#1619)    /// V.  The iterator element type is `(&K, &mut V)`.
[1620](https://docs.rs#1620)    ///
[1621](https://docs.rs#1621)    /// # Examples
[1622](https://docs.rs#1622)    ///
[1623](https://docs.rs#1623)    /// ```
[1624](https://docs.rs#1624)    /// use lru::LruCache;
[1625](https://docs.rs#1625)    /// use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
[1626](https://docs.rs#1626)    ///
[1627](https://docs.rs#1627)    /// struct HddBlock {
[1628](https://docs.rs#1628)    ///     dirty: bool,
[1629](https://docs.rs#1629)    ///     data: [u8; 512]
[1630](https://docs.rs#1630)    /// }
[1631](https://docs.rs#1631)    ///
[1632](https://docs.rs#1632)    /// let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
[1633](https://docs.rs#1633)    /// cache.put(0, HddBlock { dirty: false, data: [0x00; 512]});
[1634](https://docs.rs#1634)    /// cache.put(1, HddBlock { dirty: true,  data: [0x55; 512]});
[1635](https://docs.rs#1635)    /// cache.put(2, HddBlock { dirty: true,  data: [0x77; 512]});
[1636](https://docs.rs#1636)    ///
[1637](https://docs.rs#1637)    /// // write dirty blocks to disk.
[1638](https://docs.rs#1638)    /// for (block_id, block) in cache.iter_mut() {
[1639](https://docs.rs#1639)    ///     if block.dirty {
[1640](https://docs.rs#1640)    ///         // write block to disk
[1641](https://docs.rs#1641)    ///         block.dirty = false
[1642](https://docs.rs#1642)    ///     }
[1643](https://docs.rs#1643)    /// }
[1644](https://docs.rs#1644)    /// ```
[1645](https://docs.rs#1645)    pub fn iter_mut(&mut self) -> IterMut<'_, K, V> {
[1646](https://docs.rs#1646)        IterMut {
[1647](https://docs.rs#1647)            len: self.len(),
[1648](https://docs.rs#1648)            ptr: unsafe { (*self.head).next },
[1649](https://docs.rs#1649)            end: unsafe { (*self.tail).prev },
[1650](https://docs.rs#1650)            phantom: PhantomData,
[1651](https://docs.rs#1651)        }
[1652](https://docs.rs#1652)    }
[1653](https://docs.rs#1653)
[1654](https://docs.rs#1654)    fn remove_first(&mut self) -> Option<Box<LruEntry<K, V>>> {
[1655](https://docs.rs#1655)        let next;
[1656](https://docs.rs#1656)        unsafe { next = (*self.head).next }
[1657](https://docs.rs#1657)        if !core::ptr::eq(next, self.tail) {
[1658](https://docs.rs#1658)            let old_key = KeyRef {
[1659](https://docs.rs#1659)                k: unsafe { &(*(*(*self.head).next).key.as_ptr()) },
[1660](https://docs.rs#1660)            };
[1661](https://docs.rs#1661)            let old_node = self.map.remove(&old_key).unwrap();
[1662](https://docs.rs#1662)            let node_ptr: *mut LruEntry<K, V> = old_node.as_ptr();
[1663](https://docs.rs#1663)            self.detach(node_ptr);
[1664](https://docs.rs#1664)            unsafe { Some(Box::from_raw(node_ptr)) }
[1665](https://docs.rs#1665)        } else {
[1666](https://docs.rs#1666)            None
[1667](https://docs.rs#1667)        }
[1668](https://docs.rs#1668)    }
[1669](https://docs.rs#1669)
[1670](https://docs.rs#1670)    fn remove_last(&mut self) -> Option<Box<LruEntry<K, V>>> {
[1671](https://docs.rs#1671)        let prev;
[1672](https://docs.rs#1672)        unsafe { prev = (*self.tail).prev }
[1673](https://docs.rs#1673)        if !core::ptr::eq(prev, self.head) {
[1674](https://docs.rs#1674)            let old_key = KeyRef {
[1675](https://docs.rs#1675)                k: unsafe { &(*(*(*self.tail).prev).key.as_ptr()) },
[1676](https://docs.rs#1676)            };
[1677](https://docs.rs#1677)            let old_node = self.map.remove(&old_key).unwrap();
[1678](https://docs.rs#1678)            let node_ptr: *mut LruEntry<K, V> = old_node.as_ptr();
[1679](https://docs.rs#1679)            self.detach(node_ptr);
[1680](https://docs.rs#1680)            unsafe { Some(Box::from_raw(node_ptr)) }
[1681](https://docs.rs#1681)        } else {
[1682](https://docs.rs#1682)            None
[1683](https://docs.rs#1683)        }
[1684](https://docs.rs#1684)    }
[1685](https://docs.rs#1685)
[1686](https://docs.rs#1686)    fn detach(&mut self, node: *mut LruEntry<K, V>) {
[1687](https://docs.rs#1687)        unsafe {
[1688](https://docs.rs#1688)            (*(*node).prev).next = (*node).next;
[1689](https://docs.rs#1689)            (*(*node).next).prev = (*node).prev;
[1690](https://docs.rs#1690)        }
[1691](https://docs.rs#1691)    }
[1692](https://docs.rs#1692)
[1693](https://docs.rs#1693)    // Attaches `node` after the sigil `self.head` node.
[1694](https://docs.rs#1694)    fn attach(&mut self, node: *mut LruEntry<K, V>) {
[1695](https://docs.rs#1695)        unsafe {
[1696](https://docs.rs#1696)            (*node).next = (*self.head).next;
[1697](https://docs.rs#1697)            (*node).prev = self.head;
[1698](https://docs.rs#1698)            (*self.head).next = node;
[1699](https://docs.rs#1699)            (*(*node).next).prev = node;
[1700](https://docs.rs#1700)        }
[1701](https://docs.rs#1701)    }
[1702](https://docs.rs#1702)
[1703](https://docs.rs#1703)    // Attaches `node` before the sigil `self.tail` node.
[1704](https://docs.rs#1704)    fn attach_last(&mut self, node: *mut LruEntry<K, V>) {
[1705](https://docs.rs#1705)        unsafe {
[1706](https://docs.rs#1706)            (*node).next = self.tail;
[1707](https://docs.rs#1707)            (*node).prev = (*self.tail).prev;
[1708](https://docs.rs#1708)            (*self.tail).prev = node;
[1709](https://docs.rs#1709)            (*(*node).prev).next = node;
[1710](https://docs.rs#1710)        }
[1711](https://docs.rs#1711)    }
[1712](https://docs.rs#1712)}
[1713](https://docs.rs#1713)
[1714](https://docs.rs#1714)impl<K, V, S> Drop for LruCache<K, V, S> {
[1715](https://docs.rs#1715)    fn drop(&mut self) {
[1716](https://docs.rs#1716)        self.map.drain().for_each(|(_, node)| unsafe {
[1717](https://docs.rs#1717)            let mut node = *Box::from_raw(node.as_ptr());
[1718](https://docs.rs#1718)            ptr::drop_in_place((node).key.as_mut_ptr());
[1719](https://docs.rs#1719)            ptr::drop_in_place((node).val.as_mut_ptr());
[1720](https://docs.rs#1720)        });
[1721](https://docs.rs#1721)        // We rebox the head/tail, and because these are maybe-uninit
[1722](https://docs.rs#1722)        // they do not have the absent k/v dropped.
[1723](https://docs.rs#1723)
[1724](https://docs.rs#1724)        let _head = unsafe { *Box::from_raw(self.head) };
[1725](https://docs.rs#1725)        let _tail = unsafe { *Box::from_raw(self.tail) };
[1726](https://docs.rs#1726)    }
[1727](https://docs.rs#1727)}
[1728](https://docs.rs#1728)

[1770](https://docs.rs#1770)    len: usize,
[1771](https://docs.rs#1771)
[1772](https://docs.rs#1772)    ptr: *const LruEntry<K, V>,
[1773](https://docs.rs#1773)    end: *const LruEntry<K, V>,
[1774](https://docs.rs#1774)

[1778](https://docs.rs#1778)impl<'a, K, V> Iterator for Iter<'a, K, V> {

[1780](https://docs.rs#1780)
[1781](https://docs.rs#1781)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<(&'a K, &'a V)> {
[1782](https://docs.rs#1782)        if self.len == 0 {
[1783](https://docs.rs#1783)            return None;
[1784](https://docs.rs#1784)        }
[1785](https://docs.rs#1785)
[1786](https://docs.rs#1786)        let key = unsafe { &(*(*self.ptr).key.as_ptr()) as &K };
[1787](https://docs.rs#1787)        let val = unsafe { &(*(*self.ptr).val.as_ptr()) as &V };
[1788](https://docs.rs#1788)
[1789](https://docs.rs#1789)        self.len -= 1;
[1790](https://docs.rs#1790)        self.ptr = unsafe { (*self.ptr).next };
[1791](https://docs.rs#1791)
[1792](https://docs.rs#1792)        Some((key, val))
[1793](https://docs.rs#1793)    }
[1794](https://docs.rs#1794)
[1795](https://docs.rs#1795)    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {

[1797](https://docs.rs#1797)    }
[1798](https://docs.rs#1798)
[1799](https://docs.rs#1799)    fn count(self) -> usize {

[1801](https://docs.rs#1801)    }

[2347](https://docs.rs#2347)        assert_opt_eq(cache.get(&"pear"), "green");
[2348](https://docs.rs#2348)
[2349](https://docs.rs#2349)        // Even though we inserted "apple" into the cache earlier it has since been removed from
[2350](https://docs.rs#2350)        // the cache so there is no current value for `put` to return.
[2351](https://docs.rs#2351)        assert_eq!(cache.put("apple", "green"), None);
[2352](https://docs.rs#2352)        assert_eq!(cache.put("tomato", "red"), None);
[2353](https://docs.rs#2353)
[2354](https://docs.rs#2354)        assert!(cache.get(&"pear").is_none());
[2355](https://docs.rs#2355)        assert_opt_eq(cache.get(&"apple"), "green");
[2356](https://docs.rs#2356)        assert_opt_eq(cache.get(&"tomato"), "red");
[2357](https://docs.rs#2357)    }

[2489](https://docs.rs#2489)        for i in 0..75 {
[2490](https://docs.rs#2490)            cache.put(i, "A");
[2491](https://docs.rs#2491)        }
[2492](https://docs.rs#2492)        for i in 0..75 {

[2494](https://docs.rs#2494)        }
[2495](https://docs.rs#2495)        for i in 0..75 {
[2496](https://docs.rs#2496)            cache.put(i + 200, "C");
[2497](https://docs.rs#2497)        }
[2498](https://docs.rs#2498)        assert_eq!(cache.len(), 200);
[2499](https://docs.rs#2499)
[2500](https://docs.rs#2500)        for i in 0..75 {

[2502](https://docs.rs#2502)        }
[2503](https://docs.rs#2503)        assert_opt_eq(cache.get(&25), "A");
[2504](https://docs.rs#2504)
[2505](https://docs.rs#2505)        for i in 26..75 {
[2506](https://docs.rs#2506)            assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((i, "A")));
[2507](https://docs.rs#2507)        }
[2508](https://docs.rs#2508)        for i in 0..75 {
[2509](https://docs.rs#2509)            assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((i + 200, "C")));
[2510](https://docs.rs#2510)        }
[2511](https://docs.rs#2511)        for i in 0..75 {
[2512](https://docs.rs#2512)            assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((74 - i + 100, "B")));
[2513](https://docs.rs#2513)        }
[2514](https://docs.rs#2514)        assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((25, "A")));
[2515](https://docs.rs#2515)        for _ in 0..50 {
[2516](https://docs.rs#2516)            assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), None);
[2517](https://docs.rs#2517)        }
[2518](https://docs.rs#2518)    }

[2636](https://docs.rs#2636)    fn test_iter_forwards() {
[2637](https://docs.rs#2637)        let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
[2638](https://docs.rs#2638)        cache.put("a", 1);
[2639](https://docs.rs#2639)        cache.put("b", 2);
[2640](https://docs.rs#2640)        cache.put("c", 3);
[2641](https://docs.rs#2641)
[2642](https://docs.rs#2642)        {
[2643](https://docs.rs#2643)            // iter const
[2644](https://docs.rs#2644)            let mut iter = cache.iter();
[2645](https://docs.rs#2645)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 3);
[2646](https://docs.rs#2646)            assert_opt_eq_tuple(iter.next(), ("c", 3));
[2647](https://docs.rs#2647)
[2648](https://docs.rs#2648)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 2);
[2649](https://docs.rs#2649)            assert_opt_eq_tuple(iter.next(), ("b", 2));
[2650](https://docs.rs#2650)
[2651](https://docs.rs#2651)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 1);
[2652](https://docs.rs#2652)            assert_opt_eq_tuple(iter.next(), ("a", 1));
[2653](https://docs.rs#2653)
[2654](https://docs.rs#2654)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 0);
[2655](https://docs.rs#2655)            assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);
[2656](https://docs.rs#2656)        }
[2657](https://docs.rs#2657)        {
[2658](https://docs.rs#2658)            // iter mut
[2659](https://docs.rs#2659)            let mut iter = cache.iter_mut();
[2660](https://docs.rs#2660)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 3);
[2661](https://docs.rs#2661)            assert_opt_eq_mut_tuple(iter.next(), ("c", 3));
[2662](https://docs.rs#2662)
[2663](https://docs.rs#2663)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 2);
[2664](https://docs.rs#2664)            assert_opt_eq_mut_tuple(iter.next(), ("b", 2));
[2665](https://docs.rs#2665)
[2666](https://docs.rs#2666)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 1);
[2667](https://docs.rs#2667)            assert_opt_eq_mut_tuple(iter.next(), ("a", 1));
[2668](https://docs.rs#2668)
[2669](https://docs.rs#2669)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 0);
[2670](https://docs.rs#2670)            assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);
[2671](https://docs.rs#2671)        }
[2672](https://docs.rs#2672)    }

[2674](https://docs.rs#2674)    #[test]
[2675](https://docs.rs#2675)    fn test_iter_backwards() {
[2676](https://docs.rs#2676)        let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
[2677](https://docs.rs#2677)        cache.put("a", 1);
[2678](https://docs.rs#2678)        cache.put("b", 2);
[2679](https://docs.rs#2679)        cache.put("c", 3);
[2680](https://docs.rs#2680)
[2681](https://docs.rs#2681)        {
[2682](https://docs.rs#2682)            // iter const
[2683](https://docs.rs#2683)            let mut iter = cache.iter();
[2684](https://docs.rs#2684)            assert_eq!(iter.len(), 3);
[2685](https://docs.rs#2685)            assert_opt_eq_tuple(iter.next_back(), ("a", 1));

[2876](https://docs.rs#2876)    fn test_no_memory_leaks() {
[2877](https://docs.rs#2877)        static DROP_COUNT: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
[2878](https://docs.rs#2878)
[2879](https://docs.rs#2879)        struct DropCounter;
[2880](https://docs.rs#2880)
[2881](https://docs.rs#2881)        impl Drop for DropCounter {
[2882](https://docs.rs#2882)            fn drop(&mut self) {
[2883](https://docs.rs#2883)                DROP_COUNT.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
[2884](https://docs.rs#2884)            }
[2885](https://docs.rs#2885)        }
[2886](https://docs.rs#2886)
[2887](https://docs.rs#2887)        let n = 100;
[2888](https://docs.rs#2888)        for _ in 0..n {
[2889](https://docs.rs#2889)            let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(1).unwrap());
[2890](https://docs.rs#2890)            for i in 0..n {
[2891](https://docs.rs#2891)                cache.put(i, DropCounter {});
[2892](https://docs.rs#2892)            }
[2893](https://docs.rs#2893)        }
[2894](https://docs.rs#2894)        assert_eq!(DROP_COUNT.load(Ordering::SeqCst), n * n);
[2895](https://docs.rs#2895)    }

[2944](https://docs.rs#2944)    fn test_no_memory_leaks_with_pop() {
[2945](https://docs.rs#2945)        static DROP_COUNT: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
[2946](https://docs.rs#2946)
[2947](https://docs.rs#2947)        #[derive(Hash, Eq)]
[2948](https://docs.rs#2948)        struct KeyDropCounter(usize);
[2949](https://docs.rs#2949)
[2950](https://docs.rs#2950)        impl PartialEq for KeyDropCounter {
[2951](https://docs.rs#2951)            fn eq(&self, other: &Self) -> bool {
[2952](https://docs.rs#2952)                self.0.eq(&other.0)
[2953](https://docs.rs#2953)            }
[2954](https://docs.rs#2954)        }
[2955](https://docs.rs#2955)
[2956](https://docs.rs#2956)        impl Drop for KeyDropCounter {
[2957](https://docs.rs#2957)            fn drop(&mut self) {
[2958](https://docs.rs#2958)                DROP_COUNT.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
[2959](https://docs.rs#2959)            }
[2960](https://docs.rs#2960)        }
[2961](https://docs.rs#2961)
[2962](https://docs.rs#2962)        let n = 100;
[2963](https://docs.rs#2963)        for _ in 0..n {
[2964](https://docs.rs#2964)            let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(1).unwrap());
[2965](https://docs.rs#2965)
[2966](https://docs.rs#2966)            for i in 0..100 {
[2967](https://docs.rs#2967)                cache.put(KeyDropCounter(i), i);
[2968](https://docs.rs#2968)                cache.pop(&KeyDropCounter(i));
[2969](https://docs.rs#2969)            }
[2970](https://docs.rs#2970)        }
[2971](https://docs.rs#2971)
[2972](https://docs.rs#2972)        assert_eq!(DROP_COUNT.load(Ordering::SeqCst), n * n * 2);
[2973](https://docs.rs#2973)    }

An LRU Cache

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lru/lib.rs.html#280-282)#### pub fn [unbounded_with_hasher](https://docs.rs#method.unbounded_with_hasher)(hash_builder: S) -> [LruCache](https://docs.rs/struct.LruCache.html)<K, V, S>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lru/lib.rs.html#280-282)

#### pub fn [unbounded_with_hasher](https://docs.rs#method.unbounded_with_hasher)(hash_builder: S) -> [LruCache](https://docs.rs/struct.LruCache.html)<K, V, S>

Creates a new LRU Cache that never automatically evicts items and uses the provided hash builder to hash keys.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use lru::{LruCache, DefaultHasher};
let s = DefaultHasher::default();
let mut cache: LruCache<isize, &str> = LruCache::unbounded_with_hasher(s);
```
Puts a key-value pair into cache. If the key already exists in the cache, then it updates
the key’s value and returns the old value. Otherwise, `None` is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
assert_eq!(None, cache.put(1, "a"));
assert_eq!(None, cache.put(2, "b"));
assert_eq!(Some("b"), cache.put(2, "beta"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&1), Some(&"a"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&2), Some(&"beta"));
```
Pushes a key-value pair into the cache. If an entry with key `k` already exists in
the cache or another cache entry is removed (due to the lru’s capacity),
then it returns the old entry’s key-value pair. Otherwise, returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
assert_eq!(None, cache.push(1, "a"));
assert_eq!(None, cache.push(2, "b"));
// This push call returns (2, "b") because that was previously 2's entry in the cache.
assert_eq!(Some((2, "b")), cache.push(2, "beta"));
// This push call returns (1, "a") because the cache is at capacity and 1's entry was the lru entry.
assert_eq!(Some((1, "a")), cache.push(3, "alpha"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&1), None);
assert_eq!(cache.get(&2), Some(&"beta"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&3), Some(&"alpha"));
```
Returns a reference to the value of the key in the cache or `None` if it is not
present in the cache. Moves the key to the head of the LRU list if it exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put(1, "a");
cache.put(2, "b");
cache.put(2, "c");
cache.put(3, "d");
assert_eq!(cache.get(&1), None);
assert_eq!(cache.get(&2), Some(&"c"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&3), Some(&"d"));
```
Returns a mutable reference to the value of the key in the cache or `None` if it
is not present in the cache. Moves the key to the head of the LRU list if it exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put("apple", 8);
cache.put("banana", 4);
cache.put("banana", 6);
cache.put("pear", 2);
assert_eq!(cache.get_mut(&"apple"), None);
assert_eq!(cache.get_mut(&"banana"), Some(&mut 6));
assert_eq!(cache.get_mut(&"pear"), Some(&mut 2));
```
Returns a key-value references pair of the key in the cache or `None` if it is not
present in the cache. Moves the key to the head of the LRU list if it exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-8)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put(String::from("1"), "a");
cache.put(String::from("2"), "b");
cache.put(String::from("2"), "c");
cache.put(String::from("3"), "d");
assert_eq!(cache.get_key_value("1"), None);
assert_eq!(cache.get_key_value("2"), Some((&String::from("2"), &"c")));
assert_eq!(cache.get_key_value("3"), Some((&String::from("3"), &"d")));
```
Returns a key-value references pair of the key in the cache or `None` if it is not
present in the cache. The reference to the value of the key is mutable. Moves the key to
the head of the LRU list if it exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-9)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put(1, "a");
cache.put(2, "b");
let (k, v) = cache.get_key_value_mut(&1).unwrap();
assert_eq!(k, &1);
assert_eq!(v, &mut "a");
*v = "aa";
cache.put(3, "c");
assert_eq!(cache.get_key_value(&2), None);
assert_eq!(cache.get_key_value(&1), Some((&1, &"aa")));
assert_eq!(cache.get_key_value(&3), Some((&3, &"c")));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lru/lib.rs.html#601-606)#### pub fn [get_or_insert](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_insert)<F>(&mut self, k: K, f: F) -> [&V](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lru/lib.rs.html#601-606)

#### pub fn [get_or_insert](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_insert)<F>(&mut self, k: K, f: F) -> [&V](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)

Returns a reference to the value of the key in the cache if it is
present in the cache and moves the key to the head of the LRU list.
If the key does not exist the provided `FnOnce` is used to populate
the list and a reference is returned.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-10)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put(1, "a");
cache.put(2, "b");
cache.put(2, "c");
cache.put(3, "d");
assert_eq!(cache.get_or_insert(2, ||"a"), &"c");
assert_eq!(cache.get_or_insert(3, ||"a"), &"d");
assert_eq!(cache.get_or_insert(1, ||"a"), &"a");
assert_eq!(cache.get_or_insert(1, ||"b"), &"a");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lru/lib.rs.html#630-652)#### pub fn [get_or_insert_with_key](https://docs.rs#method.get_or_insert_with_key)<F>(&mut self, k: K, f: F) -> [&V](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)

```

Returns the value corresponding to the least recently used item or `None` if the
cache is empty. Like `peek`, `peek_lru` does not update the LRU list so the item’s
position will be unchanged.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-24)Example

Returns the value corresponding to the most recently used item or `None` if the
cache is empty. Like `peek`, `peek_mru` does not update the LRU list so the item’s
position will be unchanged.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-25)Example

```

```
Returns a bool indicating whether the given key is in the cache. Does not update the LRU list.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-26)Example

```

```
Removes and returns the value corresponding to the key from the cache or
`None` if it does not exist.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-27)Example

```

assert_eq!(cache.pop(&1), None);
assert_eq!(cache.pop(&2), Some("a"));
assert_eq!(cache.pop(&2), None);
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
```
Removes and returns the key and the value corresponding to the key from the cache or
`None` if it does not exist.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-28)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;

cache.put(1, "a");

assert_eq!(cache.pop(&1), Some("a"));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_entry(&2), Some((2, "a")));
assert_eq!(cache.pop(&1), None);
assert_eq!(cache.pop_entry(&2), None);
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
```
Removes and returns the key and value corresponding to the least recently
used item or `None` if the cache is empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-29)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put(2, "a");
cache.put(3, "b");
cache.put(4, "c");
cache.get(&3);
assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((4, "c")));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((3, "b")));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), None);
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
```
Removes and returns the key and value corresponding to the most recently
used item or `None` if the cache is empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-30)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put(2, "a");
cache.put(3, "b");
cache.put(4, "c");
cache.get(&3);
assert_eq!(cache.pop_mru(), Some((3, "b")));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_mru(), Some((4, "c")));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_mru(), None);
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
```
Marks the key as the most recently used one. Returns true if the key was promoted because it exists in the cache, false otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-31)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
cache.put(1, "a");
cache.put(2, "b");
cache.put(3, "c");
cache.get(&1);
cache.get(&2);
// If we do `pop_lru` now, we would pop 3.
// assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((3, "c")));
// By promoting 3, we make sure it isn't popped.
assert!(cache.promote(&3));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((1, "a")));
// Promoting an entry that doesn't exist doesn't do anything.
assert!(!cache.promote(&4));
```
Marks the key as the least recently used one. Returns true if the key was demoted because it exists in the cache, false otherwise.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-32)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
cache.put(1, "a");
cache.put(2, "b");
cache.put(3, "c");
cache.get(&1);
cache.get(&2);
// If we do `pop_lru` now, we would pop 3.
// assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((3, "c")));
// By demoting 1 and 2, we make sure those are popped first.
assert!(cache.demote(&2));
assert!(cache.demote(&1));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((1, "a")));
assert_eq!(cache.pop_lru(), Some((2, "b")));
// Demoting a key that doesn't exist does nothing.
assert!(!cache.demote(&4));
```

cache.put(2, "b");
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 2);

assert_eq!(cache.len(), 2);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lru/lib.rs.html#1554-1566)#### pub fn [resize](https://docs.rs#method.resize)(&mut self, cap: [NonZeroUsize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/num/nonzero/type.NonZeroUsize.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lru/lib.rs.html#1554-1566)

#### pub fn [resize](https://docs.rs#method.resize)(&mut self, cap: [NonZeroUsize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/num/nonzero/type.NonZeroUsize.html))

Resizes the cache. If the new capacity is smaller than the size of the current cache any entries past the new capacity are discarded.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-36)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache: LruCache<isize, &str> = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
cache.put(1, "a");
cache.put(2, "b");
cache.resize(NonZeroUsize::new(4).unwrap());
cache.put(3, "c");
cache.put(4, "d");
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 4);
assert_eq!(cache.get(&1), Some(&"a"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&2), Some(&"b"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&3), Some(&"c"));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&4), Some(&"d"));
```
Clears the contents of the cache.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-37)Example

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache: LruCache<isize, &str> = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
cache.put(1, "a");
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 1);
cache.put(2, "b");
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 2);
cache.clear();
assert_eq!(cache.len(), 0);
```
An iterator visiting all entries in most-recently used order. The iterator element type is
`(&K, &V)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
cache.put("a", 1);
cache.put("b", 2);
cache.put("c", 3);
for (key, val) in cache.iter() {
    println!("key: {} val: {}", key, val);
}
```
An iterator visiting all entries in most-recently-used order, giving a mutable reference on
V.  The iterator element type is `(&K, &mut V)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
struct HddBlock {
    dirty: bool,
    data: [u8; 512]
}
let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(3).unwrap());
cache.put(0, HddBlock { dirty: false, data: [0x00; 512]});
cache.put(1, HddBlock { dirty: true,  data: [0x55; 512]});
cache.put(2, HddBlock { dirty: true,  data: [0x77; 512]});
// write dirty blocks to disk.
for (block_id, block) in cache.iter_mut() {
    if block.dirty {
        // write block to disk
        block.dirty = false
    }
}
```

# lru - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lru/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/lru/

## Expand description

An implementation of a LRU cache. The cache supports `get`, `get_mut`, `put`,
and `pop` operations, all of which are O(1). This crate was heavily influenced
by the [LRU Cache implementation in an earlier version of Rust’s std::collections crate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/0.12.0/std/collections/lru_cache/struct.LruCache.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
extern crate lru;
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
fn main() {
        let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
        cache.put("apple", 3);
        cache.put("banana", 2);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"apple").unwrap(), 3);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"banana").unwrap(), 2);
        assert!(cache.get(&"pear").is_none());
        assert_eq!(cache.put("banana", 4), Some(2));
        assert_eq!(cache.put("pear", 5), None);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"pear").unwrap(), 5);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"banana").unwrap(), 4);
        assert!(cache.get(&"apple").is_none());
        {
            let v = cache.get_mut(&"banana").unwrap();
            *v = 6;
        }
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"banana").unwrap(), 6);
}
```

- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator that moves out of a `LruCache`.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator over the entries of a `LruCache`.
- [IterMut](https://docs.rs/struct.IterMut.html)
- An iterator over mutables entries of a `LruCache`.
- [LruCache](https://docs.rs/struct.LruCache.html)
- An LRU Cache

# hashbrown 0.17.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hashbrown/^0.17.0

# hashbrown

This crate is a Rust port of Google's high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash map,
adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust's standard `HashMap` and
`HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of SwissTable can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

Since Rust 1.36, the Rust standard library has adopted this implementation for
`HashMap`, using its own default hasher (see
[ std::hash::DefaultHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/hash/struct.DefaultHasher.html)).
However you may still want to use this crate instead since it works in
environments without

`std`, such as embedded systems and kernels.## Features

- Drop-in replacement for the standard library `HashMap`and`HashSet`types.
- Uses [foldhash](https://github.com/orlp/foldhash)as the default hasher, which is much faster than SipHash. However, foldhash does*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash, so if that is important to you, you might want to consider using a different hasher.
- Around 2x faster than the previous standard library `HashMap`.
- Lower memory usage: only 1 byte of overhead per entry instead of 8.
- Compatible with `#[no_std]`(but requires a global allocator with the`alloc`crate).
- Empty hash maps do not allocate any memory.
- SIMD lookups to scan multiple hash entries in parallel.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.17"
```
Then:

```
use HashMap;
let mut map = new;
map.insert;
```
## Flags

This crate has the following Cargo features:

- `nightly`: Enables nightly-only features including:- `#[may_dangle]`.
- `serde`: Enables serde serialization support.
- `rayon`: Enables rayon parallel iterator support.
- `equivalent`: Allows comparisons to be customized with the- `Equivalent`trait. (enabled by default)
- `raw-entry`: Enables access to the deprecated- `RawEntry`API.
- `inline-more`: Adds inline hints to most functions, improving run-time performance at the cost of compilation time. (enabled by default)
- `default-hasher`: Compiles with foldhash as default hasher. (enabled by default)
- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for allocators that support- `allocator-api2`. (enabled by default)

# stats_alloc 0.1.10 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/stats_alloc/0.1.*

# stats_alloc

An instrumenting middleware for global allocators in Rust, useful in testing for validating assumptions regarding allocation patterns, and potentially in production loads to monitor for memory leaks.

## Example

```
extern crate stats_alloc;
use ;
use System;
static GLOBAL: & = &INSTRUMENTED_SYSTEM;
```
## Custom allocators

Currenty wrapping a custom allocator requires the use of the nightly compiler
and compiling with the "nightly" feature due to the soon to stabilize use of
the unstable `const_fn_trait_bound` and the fact that the internals of the
instrumenting type are not public. If that's fine with you, a custom allocator
can be wrapped as follows:

```
static GLOBAL:  = new;
```

# lru 0.16.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lru/0.16.4

# LRU Cache

An implementation of a LRU cache. The cache supports `put`, `get`, `get_mut` and `pop` operations,
all of which are O(1). This crate was heavily influenced by the [LRU Cache implementation in an
earlier version of Rust's std::collections crate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/0.12.0/std/collections/lru_cache/struct.LruCache.html).

The MSRV for this crate is 1.70.0.

## Example

Below is a simple example of how to instantiate and use a LRU cache.

```
extern crate lru;
use LruCache;
use NonZeroUsize;
```

# lru 0.5.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lru/0.5.1

# LRU Cache

An implementation of a LRU cache. The cache supports `put`, `get`, `get_mut` and `pop` operations,
all of which are O(1). This crate was heavily influenced by the [LRU Cache implementation in an
earlier version of Rust's std::collections crate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/0.12.0/std/collections/lru_cache/struct.LruCache.html).

The MSRV for this crate is 1.36.0.

## Example

Below is a simple example of how to instantiate and use a LRU cache.

```
extern crate lru;
use LruCache;
```

# lru 0.18.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lru/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md

#Changelog##[v0.18.0](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.18.0) - 2026-04-27-Fix unconstrained lifetime in `get_or_insert_mut_ref`.
##[v0.17.0](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.17.0) - 2026-04-14-Upgrade `hashbrown` to 0.17.0 and update MSRV to 1.85.0.
##[v0.16.4](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.16.4) - 2026-04-13-Add `get_or_insert_with_key` and variants.
##[v0.16.3](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.16.3) - 2026-01-07-Fix Stacked Borrows violation in `IterMut`.
##[v0.16.2](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.16.2) - 2025-10-14-Upgrade hashbrown dependency to 0.16.0.
##[v0.16.1](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.16.1) - 2025-09-08-Fix `Clone` for unbounded cache.
##[v0.16.0](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.16.0) - 2025-07-02-Implement `Clone` for caches with custom hashers.
##[v0.15.0](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.15.0) - 2025-06-26-Return bool from `promote` and `demote` to indicate whether key was found.
##[v0.14.0](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.14.0) - 2025-04-12-Use `NonZeroUsize::MAX` instead of `unwrap()`, and update MSRV to 1.70.0.
##[v0.13.0](https://github.com/jeromefroe/lru-rs/tree/0.13.0) - 2025-01-27-Add `peek_mru` and `pop_mru` methods, upgrade dependency on `hashbrown` to 0.15.2, and update MSRV to 1.65.0.

# lru 0.18.0 - Docs.rs

[![Build Badge]][build status]
[![crates.io Badge]][crates.io package]
[![docs.rs Badge]][docs.rs documentation]
[![License Badge]][license]
[Documentation]
An implementation of a LRU cache. The cache supports `put`, `get`, `get_mut` and `pop` operations,
all of which are O(1). This crate was heavily influenced by the [LRU Cache implementation in an
earlier version of Rust's std::collections crate].
The MSRV for this crate is 1.85.0.
Below is a simple example of how to instantiate and use a LRU cache.
```rust,no_run
extern crate lru;
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
fn main() {
}
```
```

# hashbrown 0.17.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hashbrown/0.17.1

# hashbrown

This crate is a Rust port of Google's high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash map,
adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust's standard `HashMap` and
`HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of SwissTable can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

Since Rust 1.36, the Rust standard library has adopted this implementation for
`HashMap`, using its own default hasher (see
[ std::hash::DefaultHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/hash/struct.DefaultHasher.html)).
However you may still want to use this crate instead since it works in
environments without

`std`, such as embedded systems and kernels.## Features

- Drop-in replacement for the standard library `HashMap`and`HashSet`types.
- Uses [foldhash](https://github.com/orlp/foldhash)as the default hasher, which is much faster than SipHash. However, foldhash does*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash, so if that is important to you, you might want to consider using a different hasher.
- Around 2x faster than the previous standard library `HashMap`.
- Lower memory usage: only 1 byte of overhead per entry instead of 8.
- Compatible with `#[no_std]`(but requires a global allocator with the`alloc`crate).
- Empty hash maps do not allocate any memory.
- SIMD lookups to scan multiple hash entries in parallel.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.17"
```
Then:

```
use HashMap;
let mut map = new;
map.insert;
```
## Flags

This crate has the following Cargo features:

- `nightly`: Enables nightly-only features including:- `#[may_dangle]`.
- `serde`: Enables serde serialization support.
- `rayon`: Enables rayon parallel iterator support.
- `equivalent`: Allows comparisons to be customized with the- `Equivalent`trait. (enabled by default)
- `raw-entry`: Enables access to the deprecated- `RawEntry`API.
- `inline-more`: Adds inline hints to most functions, improving run-time performance at the cost of compilation time. (enabled by default)
- `default-hasher`: Compiles with foldhash as default hasher. (enabled by default)
- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for allocators that support- `allocator-api2`. (enabled by default)

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[https://opensource.org/license/mit](https://opensource.org/license/mit))

at your option.

# equivalent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/equivalent/^1.0/

## Expand description

[ Equivalent](https://docs.rs/trait.Equivalent.html) and

[are traits for key comparison in maps.](https://docs.rs/trait.Comparable.html)

`Comparable`These may be used in the implementation of maps where the lookup type `Q`
may be different than the stored key type `K`.

- `Q: Equivalent<K>`checks for equality, similar to the- `HashMap<K, V>`constraint- `K: Borrow<Q>, Q: Eq`.
- `Q: Comparable<K>`checks the ordering, similar to the- `BTreeMap<K, V>`constraint- `K: Borrow<Q>, Q: Ord`.

These traits are not used by the maps in the standard library, but they may
add more flexibility in third-party map implementations, especially in
situations where a strict `K: Borrow<Q>` relationship is not available.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use equivalent::*;
use std::cmp::Ordering;
pub struct Pair<A, B>(pub A, pub B);
impl<'a, A: ?Sized, B: ?Sized, C, D> Equivalent<(C, D)> for Pair<&'a A, &'a B>
where
    A: Equivalent<C>,
    B: Equivalent<D>,
{
    fn equivalent(&self, key: &(C, D)) -> bool {
        self.0.equivalent(&key.0) && self.1.equivalent(&key.1)
    }
}
impl<'a, A: ?Sized, B: ?Sized, C, D> Comparable<(C, D)> for Pair<&'a A, &'a B>
where
    A: Comparable<C>,
    B: Comparable<D>,
{
    fn compare(&self, key: &(C, D)) -> Ordering {
        match self.0.compare(&key.0) {
            Ordering::Equal => self.1.compare(&key.1),
            not_equal => not_equal,
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    let key = (String::from("foo"), String::from("bar"));
    let q1 = Pair("foo", "bar");
    let q2 = Pair("boo", "bar");
    let q3 = Pair("foo", "baz");
    assert!(q1.equivalent(&key));
    assert!(!q2.equivalent(&key));
    assert!(!q3.equivalent(&key));
    assert_eq!(q1.compare(&key), Ordering::Equal);
    assert_eq!(q2.compare(&key), Ordering::Less);
    assert_eq!(q3.compare(&key), Ordering::Greater);
}
```
## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Comparable](https://docs.rs/trait.Comparable.html)
- Key ordering trait.
- [Equivalent](https://docs.rs/trait.Equivalent.html)
- Key equivalence trait.

# foldhash - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/foldhash/^0.2.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides foldhash, a fast, non-cryptographic, minimally DoS-resistant hashing algorithm designed for computational uses such as hashmaps, bloom filters, count sketching, etc.

When should you **not** use foldhash:

-
You are afraid of people studying your long-running program’s behavior to reverse engineer its internal random state and using this knowledge to create many colliding inputs for computational complexity attacks.
-
You expect foldhash to have a consistent output across versions or platforms, such as for persistent file formats or communication protocols.
-
You are relying on foldhash’s properties for any kind of security. Foldhash is **not appropriate for any cryptographic purpose**.

Foldhash has two variants, one optimized for speed which is ideal for data
structures such as hash maps and bloom filters, and one optimized for
statistical quality which is ideal for algorithms such as
[HyperLogLog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HyperLogLog) and
[MinHash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MinHash).

Foldhash can be used in a `#![no_std]` environment by disabling its default
`"std"` feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The easiest way to use this crate with the standard library [ HashMap](https://docs.rs/type.HashMap.html) or

[is to import them from](https://docs.rs/type.HashSet.html)

`HashSet``foldhash` instead, along with the
extension traits to make [and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html#method.new)

`HashMap::new`[work out-of-the-box:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html#method.with_capacity)

`HashMap::with_capacity````
use foldhash::{HashMap, HashMapExt};
let mut hm = HashMap::new();
hm.insert(42, "hello");
```
You can also avoid the convenience types and do it manually by initializing
a [ RandomState](https://docs.rs/fast/struct.RandomState.html), for example if you are using a different hash map
implementation like

[:](https://docs.rs/hashbrown/)

`hashbrown````
use hashbrown::HashMap;
use foldhash::fast::RandomState;
let mut hm = HashMap::with_hasher(RandomState::default());
hm.insert("foo", "bar");
```
The above methods are the recommended way to use foldhash, which will
automatically generate a randomly generated hasher instance for you. If you
absolutely must have determinism you can use [ FixedState](https://docs.rs/fast/struct.FixedState.html)
instead, but note that this makes you trivially vulnerable to HashDoS
attacks and might lead to quadratic runtime when moving data from one
hashmap/set into another:

```
use std::collections::HashSet;
use foldhash::fast::FixedState;
let mut hm = HashSet::with_hasher(FixedState::with_seed(42));
hm.insert([1, 10, 100]);
```
If you rely on statistical properties of the hash for the correctness of
your algorithm, such as in [HyperLogLog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HyperLogLog),
it is suggested to use the [ RandomState](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.RandomState.html)
or

[from the](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.FixedState.html)

`FixedState`[module instead of the](https://docs.rs/quality/index.html)

`quality`[module. The latter is optimized purely for speed in hash tables and has known statistical imperfections.](https://docs.rs/fast/index.html)

`fast`Finally, you can also directly use the [ RandomState](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.RandomState.html)
or

[to manually hash items using the](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.FixedState.html)

`FixedState`[trait:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html)

`BuildHasher````
use std::hash::BuildHasher;
use foldhash::quality::RandomState;
let random_state = RandomState::default();
let hash = random_state.hash_one("hello world");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#seeding)Seeding

Foldhash relies on a single 8-byte per-hasher seed which should be ideally
be different from each instance to instance, and also a larger
[ SharedSeed](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedSeed.html) which may be shared by many different instances.

To reduce overhead, this [ SharedSeed](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedSeed.html) is typically initialized once and
stored. To prevent each hashmap unnecessarily containing a reference to this
value there are three kinds of

[s foldhash provides (both for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html)

`BuildHasher`[and](https://docs.rs/fast/index.html)

`fast`[):](https://docs.rs/quality/index.html)

`quality`- `RandomState`- `SharedSeed::global_random`
- `FixedState`- `SharedSeed::global_fixed`
- `SeedableRandomState`- `RandomState`- `SharedSeed`

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate has the following features:

- `nightly`, this feature improves string hashing performance slightly using the nightly-only Rust feature- `hasher_prefixfree_extras`
- `std`, this enabled-by-default feature offers convenient aliases for- `std`containers, but can be turned off for- `#![no_std]`crates.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [fast](https://docs.rs/fast/index.html)
- The foldhash implementation optimized for speed.
- [quality](https://docs.rs/quality/index.html)
- The foldhash implementation optimized for quality.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A random seed intended to be shared by many different foldhash instances.

- A convenience extension trait to enable `HashMap::new``foldhash`.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/trait.HashSetExt.html)- SetExt
- A convenience extension trait to enable `HashSet::new``foldhash`.

# rayon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/^1.9.0/

## Expand description

Rayon is a data-parallelism library that makes it easy to convert sequential computations into parallel.

It is lightweight and convenient for introducing parallelism into existing code. It guarantees data-race free executions and takes advantage of parallelism when sensible, based on work-load at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-rayon)How to use Rayon

There are two ways to use Rayon:

- **High-level parallel constructs**are the simplest way to use Rayon and also typically the most efficient.- [Parallel iterators](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)make it easy to convert a sequential iterator to execute in parallel.- The `ParallelIterator`
- The `IndexedParallelIterator`

- The
- The `par_sort``&mut [T]`slices (or vectors) in parallel.
- `par_extend`

- **Custom tasks**let you divide your work into parallel tasks yourself.- `join`
- `scope`
- `ThreadPoolBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-and-the-rayon-prelude)Basic usage and the Rayon prelude

First, you will need to add `rayon` to your `Cargo.toml`.

Next, to use parallel iterators or the other high-level methods,
you need to import several traits. Those traits are bundled into
the module [ rayon::prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html). It is recommended that you import
all of these traits at once by adding

`use rayon::prelude::*` at
the top of each module that uses Rayon methods.These traits give you access to the `par_iter` method which provides
parallel implementations of many iterative functions such as [ map](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.map),

[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.for_each)

`for_each`[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.filter)

`filter`[, and](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.fold)

`fold`[more](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#provided-methods).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-layout)Crate Layout

Rayon extends many of the types found in the standard library with
parallel iterator implementations. The modules in the `rayon`
crate mirror [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) itself: so, e.g., the

`option` module in
Rayon contains parallel iterators for the `Option` type, which is
found in [the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html). Similarly, the

`option` module of `std``collections` module in Rayon offers parallel iterator types for
[the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html). You will rarely need to access these submodules unless you need to name iterator types explicitly.

`collections` from `std`[§](https://docs.rs#targets-without-threading)Targets without threading

Rayon has limited support for targets without `std` threading implementations.
See the [ rayon_core](https://docs.rs/rayon-core/1.13.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rayon_core/index.html) documentation for more information about its global fallback.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-questions)Other questions?

See [the Rayon FAQ](https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/main/FAQ.md).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [broadcast](https://docs.rs/fn.broadcast.html)
- Executes `op`within every thread in the current thread pool. If this is called from a non-Rayon thread, it will execute in the global thread pool. Any attempts to use`join`,`scope`, or parallel iterators will then operate within that thread pool. When the call has completed on each thread, returns a vector containing all of their return values.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the number of threads in the current registry. If this code is executing within a Rayon thread pool, then this will be the number of threads for the thread pool of the current thread. Otherwise, it will be the number of threads for the global thread pool.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_thread_index.html)- thread_ - index
- If called from a Rayon worker thread, returns the index of that
thread within its current pool; if not called from a Rayon thread,
returns `None`.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope.html)- place_ - scope
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope_fifo.html)- place_ - scope_ - fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [join](https://docs.rs/fn.join.html)
- Takes two closures and *potentially*runs them in parallel. It returns a pair of the results from those closures.
- [join_](https://docs.rs/fn.join_context.html)- context
- Identical to `join`, except that the closures have a parameter that provides context for the way the closure has been called, especially indicating whether they’re executing on a different thread than where`join_context`was called. This will occur if the second job is stolen by a different thread, or if`join_context`was called from outside the thread pool to begin with.
- [max_](https://docs.rs/fn.max_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the maximum number of threads that Rayon supports in a single thread pool.
- [scope](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [scope_](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)- fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html)
- Puts the task into the Rayon thread pool’s job queue in the “static”
or “global” scope. Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)to create a scope.`scope()`function
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_broadcast.html)- broadcast
- Spawns an asynchronous task on every thread in this thread pool. This task
will run in the implicit, global scope, which means that it may outlast the
current stack frame – therefore, it cannot capture any references onto the
stack (you will likely need a `move`closure).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_fifo.html)- fifo
- Fires off a task into the Rayon thread pool in the “static” or
“global” scope.  Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)to create a scope.`scope_fifo()`function
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_local.html)- local
- Cooperatively yields execution to local Rayon work.
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_now.html)- now
- Cooperatively yields execution to Rayon.

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you

parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

# bumpalo - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bumpalo/^3.13.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#bumpalo)`bumpalo`

**A fast bump allocation arena for Rust.**

[§](https://docs.rs#bump-allocation)Bump Allocation

Bump allocation is a fast, but limited approach to allocation. We have a chunk
of memory, and we maintain a pointer within that memory. Whenever we allocate an
object, we do a quick check that we have enough capacity left in our chunk to
allocate the object and then update the pointer by the object’s size. *That’s
it!*

The disadvantage of bump allocation is that there is no general way to deallocate individual objects or reclaim the memory region for a no-longer-in-use object.

These trade offs make bump allocation well-suited for *phase-oriented*
allocations. That is, a group of objects that will all be allocated during the
same program phase, used, and then can all be deallocated together as a group.

[§](https://docs.rs#deallocation-en-masse-but-no-drop)Deallocation en Masse, but no `Drop`

To deallocate all the objects in the arena at once, we can simply reset the bump
pointer back to the start of the arena’s memory chunk. This makes mass
deallocation *extremely* fast, but allocated objects’ [ Drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Drop.html) implementations are
not invoked.

However:[can be used to wrap](https://docs.rs/bumpalo/latest/bumpalo/boxed/struct.Box.html)`bumpalo::boxed::Box<T>``T`values allocated in the`Bump`arena, and calls`T`’s`Drop`implementation when the`Box<T>`wrapper goes out of scope. This is similar to how[works, except without deallocating its backing memory.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html)`std::boxed::Box`

[§](https://docs.rs#what-happens-when-the-memory-chunk-is-full)What happens when the memory chunk is full?

This implementation will allocate a new memory chunk from the global allocator and then start bump allocating into this new memory chunk.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use bumpalo::Bump;
struct Doggo {
    cuteness: u64,
    age: u8,
    scritches_required: bool,
}
// Create a new arena to bump allocate into.
let bump = Bump::new();
// Allocate values into the arena.
let scooter = bump.alloc(Doggo {
    cuteness: u64::MAX,
    age: 8,
    scritches_required: true,
});
// Exclusive, mutable references to the just-allocated value are returned.
assert!(scooter.scritches_required);
scooter.age += 1;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#collections)Collections

When the `"collections"` cargo feature is enabled, a fork of some of the `std`
library’s collections are available in the [ collections](https://docs.rs/bumpalo/latest/bumpalo/collections/index.html) module. These
collection types are modified to allocate their space inside

`bumpalo::Bump`
arenas.```
#[cfg(feature = "collections")]
{
    use bumpalo::{Bump, collections::Vec};
    // Create a new bump arena.
    let bump = Bump::new();
    // Create a vector of integers whose storage is backed by the bump arena. The
    // vector cannot outlive its backing arena, and this property is enforced with
    // Rust's lifetime rules.
    let mut v = Vec::new_in(&bump);
    // Push a bunch of integers onto `v`!
    for i in 0..100 {
        v.push(i);
    }
}
```
Eventually [all  std collection types will be parameterized by an
allocator](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/42774) and we can remove
this

`collections` module and use the `std` versions.For unstable, nightly-only support for custom allocators in `std`, see the
`allocator_api` section below.

[§](https://docs.rs#bumpaloboxedbox)`bumpalo::boxed::Box`

When the `"boxed"` cargo feature is enabled, a fork of `std::boxed::Box`
is available in the `boxed` module. This `Box` type is modified to allocate its
space inside `bumpalo::Bump` arenas.

**A  Box<T> runs T’s drop implementation when the Box<T> is dropped.** You
can use this to work around the fact that

`Bump` does not drop values allocated
in its space itself.```
#[cfg(feature = "boxed")]
{
    use bumpalo::{Bump, boxed::Box};
    use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};
    static NUM_DROPPED: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
    struct CountDrops;
    impl Drop for CountDrops {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            NUM_DROPPED.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
        }
    }
    // Create a new bump arena.
    let bump = Bump::new();
    // Create a `CountDrops` inside the bump arena.
    let mut c = Box::new_in(CountDrops, &bump);
    // No `CountDrops` have been dropped yet.
    assert_eq!(NUM_DROPPED.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0);
    // Drop our `Box<CountDrops>`.
    drop(c);
    // Its `Drop` implementation was run, and so `NUM_DROPS` has been
    // incremented.
    assert_eq!(NUM_DROPPED.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 1);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Adding the `serde` feature flag will enable transparent serialization of `Vec`s, `String`s
and boxed values.

```
[dependencies]
bumpalo = { version = "3.18", features = ["collections", "boxed", "serde"] }
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use bumpalo::{Bump, boxed::Box, collections::Vec};
// Create a new bump arena.
let bump = Bump::new();
// Create a `Box`
let box = Box::new_in("hello", &bump);
// Serialize with serde_json
assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&box).unwrap(), "\"hello\"");
// Create a `Vec`
let vec = Vec::new_in( &bump);
vec.push(1);
vec.push(2);
// Serialize with serde_json
assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&vec).unwrap(), "[1, 2]");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#no_std-support)`#![no_std]` Support

Bumpalo is a `no_std` crate by default. It depends only on the `alloc` and `core` crates.

[§](https://docs.rs#std-support)`std` Support

You can optionally decide to enable the `std` feature in order to enable some
std only trait implementations for some collections:

- `std::io::Write`for- `Vec<'bump, u8>`

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-support)Thread support

The `Bump` is `!Sync`, which makes it hard to use in certain situations around
threads ‒ for example in `rayon`.

The [ bumpalo-herd](https://crates.io/crates/bumpalo-herd) crate provides a
pool of

`Bump` allocators for use in such situations.[§](https://docs.rs#nightly-rust-allocator_api-support)Nightly Rust `allocator_api` Support

The unstable, nightly-only Rust `allocator_api` feature defines an [ Allocator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/trait.Allocator.html)
trait and exposes custom allocators for

`std` types. Bumpalo has a matching
`allocator_api` cargo feature to enable implementing `Allocator` and using
`Bump` with `std` collections. Note that, as `feature(allocator_api)` is
unstable and only in nightly Rust, Bumpalo’s matching `allocator_api` cargo
feature should be considered unstable, and will not follow the semver
conventions that the rest of the crate does.First, enable the `allocator_api` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
bumpalo = { version = "3", features = ["allocator_api"] }
```
Next, enable the `allocator_api` nightly Rust feature in your `src/lib.rs` or
`src/main.rs`:

Finally, use `std` collections with `Bump`, so that their internal heap
allocations are made within the given bump arena:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use bumpalo::Bump;
// Create a new bump arena.
let bump = Bump::new();
// Create a `Vec` whose elements are allocated within the bump arena.
let mut v = Vec::new_in(&bump);
v.push(0);
v.push(1);
v.push(2);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-allocator-api-on-stable-rust)Using the `Allocator` API on Stable Rust

You can enable the `allocator-api2` Cargo feature and `bumpalo` will use [the
 allocator-api2 crate](https://crates.io/crates/allocator-api2) to implement
the unstable nightly

`Allocator` API on stable Rust. This means that
`bumpalo::Bump` will be usable with any collection that is generic over
`allocator_api2::Allocator`.[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust **1.71.1** and up. It might
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

We reserve the right to increment the MSRV on minor releases, however we will strive to only do it deliberately and for good reasons.

## Expand description

A statistics-driven micro-benchmarking library written in Rust.

This crate is a microbenchmarking library which aims to provide strong statistical confidence in detecting and estimating the size of performance improvements and regressions, while also being easy to use.

# fnv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fnv/^1.0.7/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Fowler–Noll–Vo hash function](http://www.isthe.com/chongo/tech/comp/fnv/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

The FNV hash function is a custom `Hasher` implementation that is more
efficient for smaller hash keys.

[The Rust FAQ states that](https://www.rust-lang.org/en-US/faq.html#why-are-rusts-hashmaps-slow) while the default `Hasher` implementation,
SipHash, is good in many cases, it is notably slower than other algorithms
with short keys, such as when you have a map of integers to other values.
In cases like these, [FNV is demonstrably faster](https://cglab.ca/~abeinges/blah/hash-rs/).

Its disadvantages are that it performs badly on larger inputs, and provides no protection against collision attacks, where a malicious user can craft specific keys designed to slow a hasher down. Thus, it is important to profile your program to ensure that you are using small hash keys, and be certain that your program could not be exposed to malicious inputs (including being a networked server).

The Rust compiler itself uses FNV, as it is not worried about denial-of-service attacks, and can assume that its inputs are going to be small—a perfect use case for FNV.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-fnv-in-a-hashmap)Using FNV in a `HashMap`

The `FnvHashMap` type alias is the easiest way to use the standard library’s
`HashMap` with FNV.

```
use fnv::FnvHashMap;
let mut map = FnvHashMap::default();
map.insert(1, "one");
map.insert(2, "two");
map = FnvHashMap::with_capacity_and_hasher(10, Default::default());
map.insert(1, "one");
map.insert(2, "two");
```
Note, the standard library’s `HashMap::new` and `HashMap::with_capacity`
are only implemented for the `RandomState` hasher, so using `Default` to
get the hasher is the next best option.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-fnv-in-a-hashset)Using FNV in a `HashSet`

Similarly, `FnvHashSet` is a type alias for the standard library’s `HashSet`
with FNV.

```
use fnv::FnvHashSet;
let mut set = FnvHashSet::default();
set.insert(1);
set.insert(2);
set = FnvHashSet::with_capacity_and_hasher(10, Default::default());
set.insert(1);
set.insert(2);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FnvHasher](https://docs.rs/struct.FnvHasher.html)
- An implementation of the Fowler–Noll–Vo hash function.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [FnvBuild](https://docs.rs/type.FnvBuildHasher.html)- Hasher
- A builder for default FNV hashers.
- [FnvHash](https://docs.rs/type.FnvHashMap.html)- Map
- A `HashMap`using a default FNV hasher.
- [FnvHash](https://docs.rs/type.FnvHashSet.html)- Set
- A `HashSet`using a default FNV hasher.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.9.0/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// The prelude import enables methods we use below, specifically
// Rng::random, Rng::sample, SliceRandom::shuffle and IndexedRandom::choose.
use rand::prelude::*;
// Get an RNG:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
println!("char: '{}'", rng.random::<char>());
// Try printing a random alphanumeric value instead!
println!("alpha: '{}'", rng.sample(rand::distr::Alphanumeric) as char);
// Generate and shuffle a sequence:
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
// And take a random pick (yes, we didn't need to shuffle first!):
let _ = nums.choose(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).
